hints: Notice that all the sodium ions come only from the $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ part, not from the water of crystallisation, so the % Na tells you about the anhydrous part.
Start by finding the actual mass of $\text{Na}^+$ in 35.6 g, then convert it to moles using $A_r = 23.0$ for sodium.
Use your moles of $\text{Na}^+$ to find moles and then mass of anhydrous $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, and subtract that from 35.6 g to leave the water lost.
walkthrough:
**Find the mass of sodium ions in the sample**

Think of the % by mass as a way to pick out just the sodium from the whole hydrated crystal.

$$\text{mass of Na}^+ = \frac{25.84}{100} \times 35.6 = 9.2 \text{ g}$$

**Convert sodium to moles of anhydrous sodium carbonate**

Each formula unit $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ contains 2 sodium ions, so moles of carbonate is half the moles of sodium.

$$\text{moles Na}^+ = \frac{9.2}{23.0} = 0.40 \text{ mol}$$
$$\text{moles Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = \frac{0.40}{2} = 0.20 \text{ mol}$$

**Find the mass of anhydrous salt left behind**

Now weigh that anhydrous part using $M_r(\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3) = 106.0$.

$$\text{mass Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = 0.20 \times 106.0 = 21.2 \text{ g}$$

**Get water lost by difference**

Heating drives off only water, so total mass minus anhydrous mass must be water.

$$\text{mass H}_2\text{O} = 35.6 - 21.2 = 14.4 \text{ g}$$

options.A: 7.2 g is exactly half the correct water mass. It comes from forgetting that there are 2 $\text{Na}^+$ ions per $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ and dividing by 2 twice, giving only 0.10 mol of carbonate.
options.B: 10.6 g is half the mass of anhydrous $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ (21.2 / 2). It comes from mistakenly using 1 mole of Na per mole of carbonate instead of 2, so you calculate only 0.40 mol of carbonate.
options.C: 14.4 g is correct. 9.2 g of $\text{Na}^+$ is 0.40 mol, which means 0.20 mol of $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ or 21.2 g anhydrous. 35.6 - 21.2 leaves 14.4 g of water of crystallisation driven off.
options.D: 21.2 g is the mass of anhydrous $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ that remains after heating, not the water lost. Choosing it means stopping one step too early and forgetting to subtract from 35.6 g.
